Chapter 18

Remote functions: the writes

form where a page has a button and must work without JavaScript, command where the action only exists once JavaScript is running; requested().refreshAll() for single-flight updates; invalid() with a field-bound issue; and how a form’s field names carry their types.

By the end of this chapter

Decide between form and command for a write, refresh the queries a mutation affects in the same round trip, and return a validation error to the field it belongs to.

Two flavours write. form returns an object you spread onto a <form>: it has method and action, so it works with JavaScript off, and an attachment that enhances it when JavaScript is on. command is a function you call from anywhere JavaScript is running. The rule this project follows is in the doc comment of trips.remote.ts: a page with a button is a form; a drag, a map click or a settings control is a command.

createTrip and deleteTrip redirect, because after them the person should be somewhere else — and a redirect thrown inside a form is followed by the browser whether or not JavaScript ran. updateTrip is a command, and its last line is the single-flight idea: the client that sends the command asks, in the same request, for tripBySlug to be refreshed, and requested(tripBySlug, 1).refreshAll() refreshes exactly the instances that client is holding — at most one here, and the limit is required because the list is client-controlled. The settings form in chapter 33 is the other half: updateTrip(patch).updates(tripBySlug(slug)).

addStop reads STOP_LIMIT — a number, by chapter 15 — and answers 422 when a trip is full, with a sentence the toast can show as it is: m.stop_limit({ limit: STOP_LIMIT }) is a Paraglide message with a parameter, so the limit reads “Eine Reise hat höchstens 500 Halte” on a German page. nextPosition from the domain puts the new stop after the last one on its day. returning() gives the row back so the client can select it immediately. And bump wakes the room, so everybody else’s itinerary shows the stop before the person who added it has looked up.

moveStop is chapter 12 at the wire. It takes where the card was dropped, asks place() what has to change, writes exactly those rows in one transaction, and returns the changes — the same list the browser applied optimistically. updateStop looks the stop up first because the *trip* is what authorisation is about, and a stop id alone does not say which trip. When the stop is gone — a companion removed it a moment ago — the 404 carries a sentence, m.error_no_stop(), and not the words Not found, because a toast is going to print it to a person, in their language (chapter 27 shows the toast). There is no command for “who am I”: the trip page learns whose presence chip is its own from the viewerId that tripBySlug returns with the document (chapter 26), because asking the server who you are, a moment after it rendered the page for you, is a round trip with nothing in it.

A form whose fields carry their types

The doc comment is the lesson. A form sends strings, unless a field was rendered with fields.amount.as("number"), in which case its name carries a prefix and SvelteKit coerces the value before the schema runs; a set of checkboxes rendered with fields.participants.as("checkbox", id) arrives as a string[]. So the schema is typed by the form, and the component’s as() calls are checked against it — a checkbox for a field the schema says is a number is a compile error. The amount is a decimal *here*, and becomes minor units once, with the trip’s currency, on the way into the database.

The schema itself is not in this file. ExpenseFormSchema lives in domain/schemas.ts (chapter 13), because the form in the browser runs the very same object as a *preflight* before it sends anything (chapter 31) — and a .remote.ts module may export remote functions and nothing else, so a schema defined here could not be imported there. One schema, two places it runs, no copy to drift.

invalid(issue.participants(m.issue_participants_member())) is programmatic validation: the schema cannot know whether an id belongs to a companion, the handler can, and invalid with a field-bound issue lands the message under that field in the form as if the schema had produced it — in the request’s language, because m reads the locale the middleware stored. A payer who is not on the trip is the same kind of answer, issue.paidBy(…), rather than a bare 400 that would have thrown the whole form away. The transaction writes the expense and its shares together, bump wakes the room, and watchTrip(trip.slug).reconnect() ends the handler. That last line matters: this form’s client never calls submit().updates(...), and a form handler that refreshes nothing gets SvelteKit’s default — invalidating every query and load function — which re-ran the trip page’s await tripBySlug(slug) and, now and then, held the live stream’s new document behind an await that never settled. Reconnecting the live query is the docs’ pattern for a mutation that changes what a live query shows, and because it counts as the handler’s own refresh it replaces that default.

The note is one command and one upsert — onConflictDoUpdate on the trip id — because a note is a page and last-writer-wins on a page two people rarely edit at the same moment is the honest trade against a CRDT nobody asked for. The doc comment says so and points at project 4, which built the CRDT.

The sign-in form is the one to study for error handling. One message for both “no such account” and “wrong password”, on purpose, because distinguishing them turns the form into a tool for discovering which emails have accounts. The redirect target is *sanitised* rather than rejected: it lives in a hidden field the person cannot see, so a crafted link would otherwise strand them at “invalid redirect”, and the regular expression refuses //evil.example — a protocol-relative URL that starts with a slash and still leaves the site. The password’s messages are functions, () => m.issue_password_missing(), for the reason chapter 13 gave: valibot calls a message function when the check fails, which is inside the request, where Paraglide knows the language.

If you know form actions

SvelteKit 2 had one way for a page to write: form actions — an actions export in +page.server.ts, fail() for a refusal, use:enhance from $app/forms on the <form>, and the result in page.form. They are still in SvelteKit 3 — $app/forms still exports applyAction, deserialize and enhance — and this project has none. If you are coming from them, this is the map.

Form actions (SvelteKit 2) and remote forms (SvelteKit 3)
Form actionsA remote formIn Meridian
export const actions in +page.server.ts, one per ?/nameform(schema, handler) in a .remote.ts module, spread onto the <form>createTrip, signIn, acceptInvite
fail(400, { … })invalid(issue.field(message)), landing under that fieldaddExpense, for a participant who is not on the trip
use:enhance from $app/formsnothing — the spread enhances the form; form.enhance(callback) to take overDeleteTrip.svelte
applyAction(result) and update()submit().updates(query), or the handler’s own refresh() / reconnect()the settings form; addExpense
ActionData and page.formfields — values and issues, typed by the schema — and resultevery form’s issues()
formData.get('amount') and a castfields.amount.as('number'): the name carries the typeExpenses.svelte

Underneath, both are the same request — a POST of FormData, which is why both work with JavaScript off. The difference is where it goes and what knows its shape. An enhanced action posts back to the page’s own URL, with an x-sveltekit-action: true header — the header SvelteKit reads to tell an action apart from a POST to a +server.ts on the same path. A remote form posts to its own endpoint under /_app/remote/, so there is nothing to tell apart. And the field names are SvelteKit’s to make: they carry the field’s type and the form’s id — name/1blflfo/createTrip, as a failing test’s call log prints it — so every input takes its attributes from fields.name.as('text') rather than a name written by hand.

Why this project has no form actions

Because a remote form is typed from one end to the other, and an action is typed at one end. The schema types the handler’s input and every as() call in the component, so a checkbox for a number field is a compile error; an action’s ActionData is typed from what it returns, and its inputs are strings that nobody checks until the action reads them. A remote form also lives beside the queries it refreshes, which is what makes a single-flight update one line. Form actions are not wrong — a project with a dozen of them gains nothing by rewriting them — but a new project in SvelteKit 3 starts here.

Checkpoint

  • You can say when a write is a form and when it is a command, and what each gives up.
  • You can explain single-flight mutations from both ends: requested() on the server and .updates() on the client.
  • You know how a form field’s as() type reaches the schema, and what invalid() is for.
